Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

The Price of Arab Goodwill: Why Britain Sacrificed the Jews in 1939

In May 1939, six months after Kristallnacht, Britain closed the door to Palestine. The White Paper capped Jewish immigration at 75,000 over five years, gave the Arabs a veto over everything after that, and banned or restricted Jewish land purchases in nearly the entire country. It broke the core obligations of the Mandate Britain had accepted from the League of Nations in 1922. The reason was not that Britain had changed its mind about the justice of the Jewish national home. The reason was fear.

By 1939 war with Germany was no longer a question of if, but when. Britain's survival as a world power depended on the Middle East: the Suez Canal, the route to India, and the oil of Iraq and Persia. The empire also ruled around 90 million Muslims, most of them in India, and British planners feared that a policy seen as anti-Arab in Palestine could ignite unrest across the Muslim world. Germany and Italy understood this too. Italian radio broadcast anti-British propaganda in Arabic, and German agents courted Arab nationalists. Britain could not afford an Arab world in revolt at its back while fighting in Europe.

The Arab revolt of 1936–39 had already shown what that would look like. It tied down more than 20,000 British troops and cost blood and money Britain could ill spare. Britain crushed it, but drew the lesson that the Mandate could not be enforced against the majority by force for ever, least of all with a world war approaching.

Against this, the Jews had nothing to bargain with. That was the brutal centre of the calculation.

The Jews could not switch sides; no Jew would ally with Hitler. Their loyalty was guaranteed, and guaranteed loyalty has no price.

The Arabs, by contrast, had alternatives, and alternatives are leverage.

The worlds most famous appeaser of evildoers - Neville Chamberlain - is reported to have put it bluntly in cabinet in April 1939: if Britain had to offend one side, it should be the Jews rather than the Arabs.

"It was of immense importance, from the point of view of strategy, to have the Moslem world with us. If we must offend one side, let us offend the Jews rather than the Arabs."

This commonly cited version comes from the minutes of the British Cabinet Committee on Palestine on 20 April 1939.

Britain sacrificed the Jews because they were the one party it could betray without losing.

This was appeasement applied to Palestine.

The White Paper came six months after Munich, from the same government and with the same reasoning. 

Those who threatened were accommodated; those who could not threaten were overruled. 

In Europe it meant giving Czechoslovakia to Hitler. 

In Palestine it meant closing the only door that was half-open for Europe's Jews, at the very moment when the Évian conference had shown that almost no other country would take them.

The cost was terrible. In the years that followed, refugee ships were turned away, and Jews who might have reached Palestine remained in Europe as the killing began. Britain should have suspected that outcome, and also its full scale - already in 1939. It knew the hate, violence and persecution was real, and it chose to put strategic comfort ahead of Jewish lives.

A genuine dilemma does not change what was chosen. Faced with a choice between principle of saving lots of human lives, and fear, Britain chose fear, and the price was paid by the people with the least power to object.

text:
Think of an election like a cricket match. The ruling party and the opposition parties are two competing teams.

The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) is the match umpire.

Right now, the three-member committee that picks the umpire is made up of:

The Prime Minister

A Cabinet Minister (chosen by the Prime Minister)

The Leader of the Opposition

This setup cannot be fair. 

The Prime Minister and their own minister will always vote together. That means the ruling team has 2 votes and the opposition has only 1 vote. 

In simple terms, one team gets to handpick the umpire every single time.

A Fair and Logical Way to Pick the Umpire:

To make sure no single politician controls the selection, the panel should be balanced so that no single group holds an automatic majority. 

A fair 5-member committee would look like this:

1. The Chief Justice of India (Head of the panel): 
The top judge in the country does not contest elections and has no political stake in who wins or loses.

2. The Prime Minister: 
Represents the ruling government and the mandate of the voters.

3. The Leader of the Opposition (Lok Sabha): 
Represents all non-ruling parties to balance the Prime Minister's power.

4. The Leader of the Opposition in Rajya Sabha: 
Ensures state-level interests are represented, since the Election Commission runs state elections too.

5. A Respected Retired Expert (like an ex-Chief Justice or a former CEC): Someone trusted by the public, chosen jointly by the first four members to break any tie fairly.

Two Golden Rules to Keep the CEC Honest
Even the best selection team can fail if the system has loopholes. 

Two simple rules must be put in place:

At least 4 out of 5 must agree: 
The committee should not decide by a simple majority. If at least 4 members must sign off—including the top judge—politicians will be forced to choose an honest, neutral person acceptable to everyone.

No government jobs after retirement: Once a CEC retires, they should be banned from accepting gifts like governorships, Rajya Sabha seats, or government appointments. 

An umpire who hopes for a prize from the ruling party after the match ends will never be fully neutral during the match.

India can fix 50% of its problems if the government implements just three laws.

1. If you want Govt Job, it should be made compulsory to send your kids to Govt Schools only as long as you are in Govt job  

2. Same should be done with Politicians, MPs, MLAs and they shouldn't get elected more than 2 terms.
  
3. Private hospitals should be banned for all bureaucrats, politicians and judges.

It should be law.

Managing Coins & Currency

Confusing coin-sizes

Presently there are three sizes each in coins of denominations of rupees one and two, creating big confusion amongst members of public. One-rupee coin is in circulation in diameters of 20, 22 and 25 mms, while coins in denominations of rupees two in circulation are 23, 25 and 27 mms. Such nearing or same sizes of coins in denominations of rupees one and two cause big confusion. To remove all confusions, central government should stop minting two-rupee coins at least for time being. Practically only varying sizes of two-rupee coins create confusion. System should be that either coins or currency-notes should only be issued in any of the denominations. Weights of coins in denominations of rupees 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 respectively should be rationalised in round figures of 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 gms respectively.

Currency-size should be reduced

Size of currency-notes was changed after the year 1967 between the years 2016 to 2019 after new currency-set was issued due to demonetisation of old currency-notes of rupees 500 and 1000 on 08.11.2016. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) should ensure that, currency-size if required to be changed, may be done in one go for notes of all denominations. With printing of notes in denominations of rupees 1 and 10 already discontinued, printing of rupees 20 notes should also be discontinued after coins of this denomination are now popular in circulation, thus paving way for new smaller-sized currency of rupees 50, 100, 200 and 500 but retaining colours of these notes same respectively in different denominations to avoid confusion amongst members of public.

Plastic currency (then for ten-rupee notes) was stated to be issued long back by the then Union Minister of State for Finance Namo Narain Meena on 12.03.2013 in a written reply in Rajya Sabha. But it was never implemented. It is good that ultimately it has been decided to issue some particular denominations of notes in plastic form. Instead of introducing rupees 10 and 20 notes in plastic currency, rupees 50 notes should be issued in plastic currency with reduced size. Since coins of rupees 10 And 20 have become popular, printing of rupees 10 and 20 notes should be altogether discontinued. Plastic currency prevailing in several countries are found successful increasing lives of currency notes manifolds. Fifty-rupee currency-notes of plastic may be issued on experimental basis. If idea becomes successful, then currency-notes of all other denominations can be issued in plastic currency. These steps will reduce cost on currency-circulation.

Introduce smaller coin-packs of 100 coins in every bank-branch

Smaller packs of 100 coins in each denomination should be always made available in plenty at all branches of various private and public sector banks and in all post-offices for ease of normal public. Bigger packs can have twenty small packs of 100 coins each thus having a uniform bigger pack-size of 2000 coins in each denomination rather than as at present in confusing pack-sizes of 2000 and 2500 coins. It is observed that even bigger bank-branches equipped with currency-chests usually do not have coins of desired denominations. Unwanted coins of rupee-two denominations are however always available, thus making gimmick popularity of two-rupee coins.

Ban sale of coin-bags and new currency by private dealers on premium

Selling coin-bags of new coins and also new packs of currency at premium should be altogether banned. These are openly sold at heavy premium depending on demand and supply. Re-introduced one-rupee note packs of 100 on 06.03.2015 never-never reached at bank-counters for public-distribution, but were always available right from 06.03.2015 at heavy premium with private dealers of new currency.

Only very few were aware of one-rupee notes were re-issued on 06.03.2015 after being discontinued two decades back. It is significant that only one-rupee notes bear signature of a secretary-rank officer of central government, while notes in all other denominations bear signature of RBI governor. Evidently one-rupee note was re-issued for bureaucratic craze to sign these notes. Even though printing of one-rupee notes has since been discontinued, enquiry should be initiated on re-issue of these one-rupee notes on 06.03.2015 with existing print-stock sold by RBI as souvenir in attractive plastic-packs so that government rather than currency-dealers may earn as premium on one-rupee notes.

Commemorative silver-alloy coins should have realistic face-value to be issued on face-value

First silver-alloy commemorative coin with face-value of rupees ten in independent India was made available for general public at face-value right from the date of issue on 02.10.1969 on Gandhi Birth Centenary. Metal-value at that time in silver-alloy coin used to be about half the face-value. This practice continued for several years. But later the practice was changed to have face-value much-much less than the prevailing metal-value.  For example, silver-alloy commemorative coins issued on 24.12.2018 to mark birth-anniversary of late Prime Minister Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee had face-value of just rupees 100 whereas metal-value of the coin even at time of issue was multiple times the face-value. It should be ensured that these coins may be issued on face-value by making it say rupees 1000 with metal-value being about half of face-value of the coin. However, to prevent fake and duplicate coins, these high-value silver-alloy coins can be packed in tamper-proof plastic-packs with serial-numbers. Commemorative coins whenever issued, should be in all commonly circulated denominations like of rupees one, five, ten and twenty also so that the occasion may be really commemorated by masses also through issue of commemorative coins. Official commemorative gold-coins of five and ten gms with 80-percent gold and 20-percent silver in face-values of rupees 5000 and 10000 respectively can also be issued in attractive tamperproof plastic-packs with serial numbers.

Sale of commemorative coin-sets should start right from date of release

Only one (say costliest Proof category) of coin-set with all denominations of coins issued on the occasion should be simultaneously released for affording coin-collectors at convenient distribution-centres like including all RBI offices, selected bank-branches (private and public sector), all philatical counters right from date of issue rather through cumbersome procedure of advance-booking with booking started much later after date of issue of commemorative coins with actual delivery of coin-sets still later at times after about a year. Information received under RTI Act reveals that at times commemorative coin-sets are booked only in some hundreds. All such steps will tremendously increase sale of commemorative coins and coin-sets thus generating appreciable revenue-earning since such high-value coins and coin-sets never come in circulation.

First-ever sale-counter for commemorative silver-alloy coins was opened on 20.01.2020 at office of Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Limited (SPMCIL) at Jawahar Vyapar Bhawan (Janpath - New Delhi) with some coin-sets put on direct sale without any advance-booking. But just one sale-counter in a big country with population of 140 crores is not enough. Sale of coin-sets should also be through credit and debit cards also. Sale of round-shaped silver or gold coins prepared in private sector should then be banned to further prevent manufacture of fake and duplicate coins.

Currency-notes should carry photos of freedom-fighters of pre-independence India

A Division Bench at Madurai of Madras High Court on 04.02.2021 had recommended to consider printing photo of Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose on currency-notes. An altogether new series of currency notes should be issued in different denominations with note of each denomination having photo of one pre-independence hero who might have expired before independence to avoid political controversies. Likewise, photos of different dignitaries can be embossed on commonly-circulated coins of different denominations.

text:
Following the arrest of Jai Singh Rathore, also known as Ajayvir Singh, various UP Police social-media handles have continued to post updates about the case. According to the police, Rathore allegedly sought money from people by claiming that his sister was seriously ill, while the investigation reportedly found that he did not have a sister.

When people came forward to help him, an X account allegedly provided him with ₹35,000. Subsequently, claims emerged that the same account was allegedly involved in betting promotion or related activities through X and Telegram. After this alleged connection became a subject of discussion on social media, the account was reportedly locked and is said to remain locked.

After the implementation of PROGA, legal real-money gaming operations falling within its scope were shut down. Yet nearly a year later, questions remain about offshore betting platforms allegedly targeting Indian users and the promotional networks connecting them to these platforms.

The potential user journey can be relatively simple:

Social Media → Influencer/Promoter → Telegram/Private Channel → Referral Link → Offshore Betting Platform → Payment

Influencers with millions of followers can potentially bring these promotions to a huge audience, including young users. The issue therefore goes beyond individual advertisements. It concerns the wider affiliate and referral ecosystem behind them.

Who pays these promoters? Where do referral commissions come from? Who operates the accounts promoting these platforms? And who is tracking the movement of users from Instagram and X to Telegram and ultimately to offshore betting websites?

The money trail is equally important.

When Indian users make payments, which entities ultimately receive the funds? Are intermediaries, wallets, third-party accounts or other payment routes being used? Who are the actual beneficial owners of these operations?

Blocking a website may address only one part of the problem. A network can potentially reappear through new domains, social-media accounts, Telegram channels and payment routes. Effective enforcement would therefore require following the network and its financial links, rather than focusing only on individual websites.

There is also a consumer-protection concern. Aggressive betting promotion can expose young users to financial losses and debt. In serious cases, financial pressure may be associated with further unlawful behaviour, although such a connection should not be assumed in every individual case.

This leaves several questions for the government and investigative agencies:

- How many offshore betting platforms are targeting Indian users?
- How many domains have been blocked over the past year, and how quickly are replacement domains appearing?
- How many social-media accounts and influencers have been investigated for betting promotion?
- How are movements from Instagram/X to Telegram and offshore platforms being monitored?
- Through which payment routes are funds reaching offshore operators?
- Who are the actual beneficial owners behind these platforms and promotional networks?
- What action has been taken against repeat promoters and bookmakers?

Most importantly, what has actually changed on the ground nearly a year after the implementation of PROGA?

The debate should not be limited to legal RMG versus illegal betting. If regulated real-money gaming operations have been acted against while offshore betting networks continue to reach Indian users through social media, messaging platforms and influencers, that potential enforcement gap deserves serious investigation.

The central issue is not simply the reach of an individual account. It is whether an offshore betting ecosystem targeting Indian users is continuing to operate—and, if so, whether authorities are effectively tracking its promoters, operators, payment routes and beneficiaries.

text:
WHEN CRITICISM DISAPPEARS, DEMOCRACY NEEDS ANSWERS

A troubling question is emerging around the removal of social-media content critical of those in power:

Who decides what gets taken down—and on what specific legal grounds?

Peek TV says one of its ground reports was removed following an order attributed to the Delhi Police. According to the video, the notice accused accounts of sharing edited or fake propaganda and attempting to incite protests, but the creators say it did not identify a specific violation in their report.

This is where transparency becomes essential.

Section 69A of the IT Act does provide a legal framework for blocking online information. But the Supreme Court's 2015 Shreya Singhal judgment upheld that framework subject to safeguards, including recorded reasons for blocking so that affected parties can challenge the decision.

And this is not merely a theoretical concern. In April 2026, the Delhi High Court directed authorities in another social-media blocking matter to identify the specific objectionable material and pass a reasoned order.

So the democratic demand is straightforward:

Show the order.
State the specific violation.
Provide the legal basis.
Allow the affected creator to challenge it.

If content is genuinely unlawful, due process should establish that.

If it is journalism, criticism or satire that has been wrongly removed, due process should protect it.

Either way, secretive or unexplained censorship weakens public trust.

A democracy should be strong enough to face criticism—and transparent enough to explain every restriction placed on speech.

QUESTION. VERIFY. DEMAND DUE PROCESS.

text:
DELHI HC RECORDS APOLOGIES BY TWO DEFENDANTS IN ARUN MEHTA DEFAMATION SUIT; NAMES DELETED FROM CASE

New Delhi: The Delhi High Court on September 30 recorded that Defendant Nos. 3 and 5 in a civil suit filed by former Jammu and Kashmir Chief Secretary Arun Kumar Mehta had published apologies concerning the article at the centre of the dispute. Following the plaintiff’s request, Justice Manoj Jain ordered that their names be deleted from the array of parties in CS(OS) 859/2025.

The court order records that counsel for Mehta informed the court that the two defendants had “realized their mistake” and published apologies with respect to the article. Mehta, who was present in person, also stated that he was no longer interested in pursuing the case against them. The court accordingly directed that Defendant Nos. 3 and 5 be deleted from the array of parties and that an amended Memo of Parties be filed.

The development comes as the remaining defendants continue to contest the proceedings. The court allowed the written statements of Defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 to be taken on record after applications seeking condonation of delay, subject to each defendant paying costs of Rs 10,000 to the plaintiff within four weeks.

During the proceedings, counsel for Mehta further submitted that the plaintiff would withdraw his case against the other defendants if they tendered a similar apology. Defendant No. 4 sought time to consider the proposal. The matter has been listed for further consideration on December 15, 2026.

Advocate Vasudev Sharan Swain, representing Mehta, said the apologies marked an important development in the case and that the plaintiff would continue to pursue the proceedings against defendants who do not apologise and continue to stand by the disputed allegations.

The plaintiff has also maintained that the apologies vindicate his stand that the allegations published against him were unfounded and caused damage to his reputation. These assertions, however, are the plaintiff’s position in the litigation and are not a finding on the merits recorded in the September 30 order.

The order was passed by Justice Manoj Jain in CS(OS) 859/2025 on September 30, 2026.

text:
India's platforms are legally required to notify users when their content gets taken down by government order — but compliance is spotty at best.
The rule exists under the Information Technology Act's intermediary framework. When a platform receives a government takedown notice, users are supposed to get an explanation: what was removed, why, and which authority issued it.
In practice, most platforms either ignore this entirely or send vague notices after the fact. No timeline is enforced. No standardized format exists. Users often discover their content is gone only when they try to access it.
Former MeitY (Ministry of Electronics and IT) cyber-law officials have flagged this gap repeatedly. The logic was simple: transparency about state censorship creates a paper trail, deters overreach, and lets users contest removals.
But India's digital ecosystem treats the notification rule as optional. WhatsApp doesn't notify for group bans. Twitter (now X) batches notices weeks later. YouTube compliance varies by region. TikTok, before its ban, rarely proactively informed users.
The enforcement gap matters because:
• There is no penalty structure — platforms face no fines or license consequences for skipping notification.
• Users have no realistic way to challenge removals without knowing they happened or why.
• Government agencies know the lack of oversight means takedowns go undocumented.
• A parallel system of private censorship operates without the judicial review that formal bans would trigger.
The fix would require either stricter intermediary rules with real penalties, or a centralized notification registry — both politically difficult in India's current regulatory environment.
As government content moderation requests accelerate globally, India's notification gap is becoming a template for how to make state censorship functionally invisible.

In Shaurya Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab & Another & connected matters, CWP-34296-2024, pronounced on 01.10.2026, the Punjab & Haryana High Court has laid down an important framework for application of Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act.

✅ Validity of Section 16(2)(c) read with Section 155 upheld, but the provision cannot be used in isolation to automatically reverse ITC merely because the supplier failed to pay tax. The officer must examine the genuineness of the transaction and surrounding circumstances.

🚫 Supplier cancellation, nil/short tax payment or departmental alerts are only triggers for inquiry — they are not, by themselves, sufficient grounds for ITC denial.

🔍 Before proceeding against the buyer, the Department must examine the supplier, invoices, relevant tax period, nature of default and recovery action already taken against the supplier.

📑 Where fraud is alleged under Section 74/74A, the SCN itself must contain facts connecting the purchaser with such fraud; supplier-side fraud cannot simply be transferred to the recipient.

🧾 Though the purchaser bears the burden under Section 155, eligibility may be established through invoices, e-way bills, transport documents, weighbridge slips, stock/consumption records and proof of actual receipt of supplies.

💰 Double recovery is impermissible. Tax already recovered from/deposited by the supplier must be considered, along with permissible re-availment of ITC; importantly, the law applicable to the relevant tax period must be applied.

👂 Taxpayers are entitled to personal hearing and a reasoned speaking order; where third-party statements are relied upon, a request for cross-examination must be considered by a reasoned order.

🛑 For the pending batch, taxpayers at SCN stage were allowed 8 weeks to file supplementary replies/evidence, and the Court directed that no fresh coercive recovery action be taken until fresh decisions are passed.

📌 Key Takeaway: Section 16(2)(c) remains valid, but ITC cannot be reversed mechanically. Supplier default must be examined through proper investigation, taxpayer evidence and due process before liability is fastened on the purchaser.

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon @Meta to remove restrictions on Satish Acharya’s posts and account and Manjul’s Instagram posts with immediate effect. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions on cartoons and satirical content. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

Timeline Of Rafale Mystery & A Saffron Chief Justice 

📍On 18 November 2016, the #Modi Govt told #Parliament that the cost of each #Rafale would be ₹670 crore.

📍On 31 December 2016, Dassault Aviation's annual report revealed that the actual price paid for each of the 36 aircraft was about ₹1,600 crore, more than twice what the #Modi Govt of India had said it was.

📍On 13 March 2017, Parrikar resigned as Defence Minister.

📍On 14 May 2017, Hollande's term as #French President ended.

📍On 13 March 2018, a PIL was filed in the #SupremeCourt which asked the #Modi Govt to disclose the transaction cost, and also asked why the Cabinet's approval was not sought as part of the Defence Procurement Procedure before signing the procurement deal with #France on 23 September 2016.

📍On 22 September 2018, Former French President Hollande was quoted in an interview as saying that it was the #Modi Govt that had insisted on Dassault partnering with #AnilAmbani for Rafale. 

📍The next day, 23 September, Hollande confirmed what he had said, and added that the name of #Reliance appeared as part of a 'new formula' by the #Modi Govt after it came to power.

📍On 10 October 2018, the #SupremeCourt asked the #Modi Govt to file in a 'sealed cover', details of the Rafale agreement.

⚠️ On 23 October 2018, at 2 a.m. in the morning, Modi divested #CBI chief Alok Verma of his powers, apparently after he showed interest in filing an FIR on the Rafale matter.

📍On 12 November 2018, the Union gave the pricing details in a 'Sealed Cover'.

📍On 14 December 2018, the #SupremeCourt dismissed all petitions asking the CBI to file an FIR in the deal. The bench, headed by CJI #RanjanGogoi.

📍On 2 January 2019, Jaswant Sinha, Arun Shourie and Prashant Bhushan moved court seeking a review of the 14 December judgement.

📍On 10 January 2019, the #SupremeCourt reinstated #CBI chief Alok Verma. 
⚠️ The next day, the #Modi Govt transferred him out of the #CBI and into the Fire Services.

📍On 14 November 2019, the #SupremeCourt dismissed the review pleas and said there was no need for an FIR.

💥 #RanjanGogoi retired three days later on 17 November, and was immediately appointed to the #rajyasabha. 

Thus Ended the Saga of the Rafale Deal.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

A Possible Explanation:

The US knew there was a threat to RAF Fairford - that's not in dispute here. The FPCON changes, armed patrol vehicles inside the base and concrete barricades all show that.

It seems possible to me that perhaps these 5 lads (or 8-10 if the eyewitness farmer is correct) were not actually there to attack the base - perhaps (given the fake fuel vans) they were actually in the area trying to steal fuel from local vehicles.

The farmer sees it, calls police. Police (who likely were aware of the USAF concerns) swarm into the area having perhaps not expected the "attackers" so soon. They manage to arrest 5 suspects and treat the 3 vans with every necessary precaution (as they should) - evacuating the neighbourhood, bringing Army EOD in, etc.

The males are initially arrested for Explosives Act offences (pending a safe way to check inside the vans) & go to custody. In the circumstances, further arrested for the Terrorism Act offence. However, after seizing whatever evidence they could (and examining the vans), it looks like police may have determined these aren't the attackers - as I say, potentially fuel thieves in the wrong place at the wrong time?

It's worth noting that if the terrorism act offences were looking likely, police could keep them detained for 48hrs initially before requiring a court to approve a longer period of time. Alternatively under normal arrest powers contained within the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, they can be held for 24hrs initially (extended to 36hrs under authority of a Police Superintendent if specific requirements are met), and up to 72hrs if a further extension is authorised by a court. Now clearly if they were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning and conveyed either to a local custody, or a dedicated counter-terrorism custody (likely closest in London), the fact they've been bailed today suggests they've spent at most 24-30hrs in custody before evidential review officers and the Crown Prosecution Service have determined there is insufficient evidence to charge them with an offence right now.

So they bail them with conditions not to contact each other as is normal procedure for vehicle interference/theft offences like that. But police need to download and analyse phones, and anything potentially seized from home addresses in order to ensure no link to the Iranian government or IRGC.

Meanwhile, did the actual planned attack get foiled inadvertently? Perhaps? Trump told the world that the US had been monitoring the "attackers" for some time - I'd suggest that if these lads genuinely were just in the wrong place at the wrong time, the actual suspects are now staying hidden until this all blows over a bit.

Either way, we don't have all the facts and that's part of any criminal or CT investigation - so yes, it sounds bad and arguably CTP could have done a better job of explaining it to the public, but they have to play their cards close to their chest right now in case my guesswork here is right and the suspects are still out there somewhere.

The “Super Intelligence” moment is, at its core, a branding exercise with a thin but real governance layer underneath. The rename is fluff — a presidential decree to swap one term for another across federal documents. The White House Accord and the U.S.-China dialogue, however, are not nothing, though they stop well short of what a technology this powerful demands.

First, the terminology shift. Trump ordered all executive branch agencies to use “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence,” a move Xi signed onto during the UN visit. The administration itself framed the rename as a substantive agreement: a Gizmodo report notes the official document says “the two leaders agreed to use the term ‘super intelligence’ … to describe the application.” But there’s no enforcement beyond U.S. federal paperwork, and industry, researchers, and the rest of the world are unlikely to follow — one public comment correctly points out the term already has a different meaning in AI safety circles, where “superintelligence” refers to systems radically smarter than humans, not the current crop of chatbots and data centres. So the rename is optically clever — it signals seriousness and shares a talking point with China — but it muddies the technical conversation and creates a small domain-name bubble (Slovenia’s .si registrations spiking), not a policy breakthrough.

Second, the substantive output: the 308-word “White House Accord on Super Intelligence.” According to Forbes, it includes “four layers of controls and audits” that companies voluntarily agreed to. The New York Times described Trump’s stance as asking A.I. titans to “police themselves,” and NBC quoted him calling for “tremendous self-regulation.” So the accord is a voluntary industry pledge, not a regulatory framework. That might be better than nothing — a public commitment with some audit layers could create a floor for responsible behaviour — but history with voluntary tech pledges (data privacy, election integrity) is mixed at best. The accord’s thinness, combined with Trump’s explicit rejection of a joint U.S.-China AI venture (BBC report), suggests the administration is drawing a hard line: cooperate on incident communication, but compete on development. That’s a coherent position, but it leaves the hardest problems — alignment, misuse, runaway scaling — to self-interested corporate actors.

Third, the geopolitical dimension. Last week’s U.S.-China deal to establish a “super intelligence” dialogue and a communications channel for serious incidents is arguably more consequential than the White House event. An Axios article from Sept. 26 describes it as a way to “help defuse serious incidents.” In a scenario where an AI system causes a market crash, a military near-miss, or a critical infrastructure failure, having a direct line between the two AI superpowers could be genuinely valuable. Yet the same day the Axios piece ran, Trump was ruling out joint ventures, and the White House accord is entirely domestic. So we have a two-track approach: talk about incidents, but don’t share technology. The risk is that the dialogue becomes a fig leaf — a channel that exists but never gets used proactively, while each side races ahead.

Fourth, the White House meeting itself. The video transcript shows Trump’s characteristic framing: “the greatest most brilliant people probably in the world,” “we love our country,” a nod to Japan, and the claim that the industry “could be substantially bigger” than the industrial revolution. Notable for what’s missing: any mention of red lines, compute caps, existential risk, or even the specific layers of the accord. The meeting was a lunch with “nearly 20 tech titans” (NBC) — a who’s who of compute and software leaders — and the outcome was a short, voluntary document. For an issue that some of those same executives have publicly called a risk on par with nuclear weapons, that’s a mismatch of scale.

Worth addressing the counter-argument: maybe this is the best that can be achieved in a divided political climate. The CNBC piece notes Trump’s polls are sinking, so the White House may have wanted a quick, positive narrative. The accord gets big names in a room and produces a symbolic win without a legislative fight. And a U.S.-China dialogue that normalises communication is not trivial — it was exactly this kind of channel that helped prevent Cold War escalations. But even a sympathetic reading can’t avoid the conclusion that the actual risk-management tools on the table — voluntary audits, a phone line — are far from proportional to an industry that the president himself compares to the industrial revolution.

My net judgment: the “Super Intelligence” rebrand is cosmetic; the accord is a modest step that signals industry awareness but lacks teeth; the U.S.-China dialogue is the most promising piece, provided it’s followed by actual protocols and not just photo ops. The real test is whether the four layers of audits have meaningful third-party oversight and public transparency, or whether they become another internal compliance checklist. If within a year we see concrete incident-reporting mechanisms and at least one audit finding made public, this week will look like a foundation. If not, it will rightly be remembered as a very expensive lunch.

――――――
